query: Can an 8-Person StartUp Sell to a CIO? Yes — If You Understand The Social Contract.
answer:
I was at Dreamforce a few years ago when I had my first interaction with a CIO. It was a big deal for me because up until then I'd never met a CIO. Never really heard what they thought, how they think, and what their problems were. And this particular CIO just kind of blew me away by saying something like "I used to buy Salesforce licenses myself, now we have such a large enterprise agreement that nobody knows where all those seats actually go."
And he said, "We're going through budget cuts right now, so we need to reduce our headcount." He looked around the room and said, "That means some people here will lose their jobs today."
He walked out of the meeting room and the rest of us sat there in stunned silence. We didn't know quite what to do next. But that moment was formative for me. It taught me that software executives work under different social contracts than consumer companies and even most SaaS companies. Their job security comes from delivering on-time features, building reliable systems, reducing operational complexity, and demonstrating clear value over time. Not from shipping great products quickly, growing fast, or achieving perfect unit economics.
The CIO's Job Is Getting Harder
Let me tell you why CIOs matter more than ever:
They've been doing layoffs every quarter since '22
Their budgets have shrunk significantly in real terms
CFOs have taken control of IT spending decisions across the board
There are fewer and fewer new tech vendors being allowed into organizations
It's harder to get meetings with CIOs
Mostly they don't want to meet with start-ups anymore
Many top CIOs have moved to a "cut-cut" mode - cutting everything
But despite all this, AI isn't getting any easier.

evidence.text:
So there’s a strategy exercise I like to go through with startups I’ve invested in that are past $20m-$30m ARR or so:
Who would you buy with 10% of your market cap?
I.e., who would you give 10% of your company away to buy?  It turns out this is an important threshold.  The SEC generally defines this as “material”.  It’s also enough of your company that everyone will suffer a lot of dilution, and enough that you can’t do more than a handful of these deals ever.  Versus later, when you are bigger, you can do a ton of tiny acquisitions.  If you are worth $10 Billion and buy a small startup for, say $50m, really, you’ll never notice the dilution or, in some cases, even the cash spent.
But I like this exercise because it focuses founders that are starting to achieve scale on maybe just one out-of-the-box idea for combining with someone to do something even bigger and better.
And now is a good time to think about this.  Times are tougher, and egos are muted.  Now might be a good time to buy one of your top partners, a smaller but scrappier competition, or someone that’s built that key part of your vision that you yourself haven’t been able to build.
Mark Zuckerberg did this twice.  He paid 10% of Facebook’s stock for WhatsApp, and 10% for Instagram.  He knew.  He knew those deals, while big ones, would add far more than 10% value to Facebook.  Imagine, indeed, where Facebook would be today without either of them.

Some are approaching 1x. CS Disco might be the 1x ARR canary in the coal mine. But it won’t be the last. Think about the math. If you’re a B2B company doing $100-200M in revenue, growing single digits, still not profitable, and you’re competing against AI-native startups that are growing 300-400% with hundreds of millions in VC backing — what’s your terminal multiple? The answer might be 1x. Or less. It might just be your cash balance. That’s the real fear. Not that these companies go bankrupt — most have years of runway. But that the public market essentially says:
we’ll pay you book value for your cash and your customer base, and nothing for the software itself, because we think AI-native competitors will eventually take it. This is different from previous B2B corrections. In 2022-2023, multiples compressed because interest rates went up and growth slowed. But the underlying assumption was still that these were durable, defensible software businesses. What’s happening now is more existential. The market is starting to question whether pre-AI SaaS platforms have structural defensibility at all when a three-year-old startup can rebuild the core functionality on top of frontier models and sell it at a fraction of the price.

DISCO is a $155M revenue company with real customers, real gross margins, and a real AI product. And the market values the business itself — net of cash — at roughly what Harvey raises in a single funding round. If you’re running a pre-AI B2B company growing under 10%, this should keep you up at night. Because CS Disco says: yes, 1x ARR — or even just 1x cash — might be where this ends. The only way out is to either accelerate growth dramatically, get acquired before the market fully reprices you, or prove that your AI capabilities are genuinely competitive with the AI-native players.
